opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most important questions right now, and honestly it's a problem that exists already with humans in the loop. Automation just makes it much sharper.

Look at how RL research has worked for the last ten years. We have a handful of benchmarks, Atari, MuJoCo, some grid worlds, and the whole community iterates against them. Every paper is effectively another sample from a giant hyperparameter and algorithm search, and the publication process acts as the selection step. So even without anyone doing anything dishonest, you get a kind of collective overfitting. You end up with methods that are very good at the quirks of those environments, the specific reward scales, the specific episode lengths, and not necessarily good at the thing we actually care about, which is general learning ability.

Now imagine you replace the grad students with an automated system that can propose and evaluate thousands of ideas a day. That is basically a massively more powerful optimizer pointed at the same narrow target. And we know what happens when you put a strong optimizer on a proxy: Goodhart's law hits you hard. The system will find every shortcut, every evaluation bug, every bit of leakage between training and test. In some sense it's reward hacking at the meta level. The research agent is being trained or selected on "make the number go up," and it will do exactly that.

So how do I think about mitigating it? A few things.

First, the evaluation has to be open-ended rather than static. If your benchmark is a fixed set of environments, it's going to get saturated and exploited. You want procedurally generated environments, or better yet, distributions of environments that themselves adapt, so the target keeps moving. That's part of why I'm excited about things like JAX-based environments that run end to end on accelerators. You can generate and evaluate on huge numbers of tasks cheaply, so you can afford truly held-out distributions.

Second, you need proper held-out evaluation at the level of the research process, not just the model. The discovered algorithm should be tested on environments the discovery system never touched, ideally ones that are structurally different. We've seen in meta-learned optimizers and learned RL objectives that the interesting question isn't how well it does on the meta-training distribution, it's how far it transfers. If it only works in-distribution, you haven't discovered an algorithm, you've discovered a lookup table.

Third, and this is the more philosophical point, I think we should treat the automated scientist as an agent with its own incentives, because it effectively has them. That means thinking about it in multi-agent and mechanism design terms. What's the incentive structure? Can you have adversarial evaluators whose job is to break the claimed result? Science works, when it works, because people are rewarded for finding flaws in each other's work. We'd want to build some of that adversarial pressure into the automated pipeline as well.

And finally, interpretability of the outputs matters a lot. If an automated system hands you an algorithm, you want to be able to read it, understand why it works, and form your own hypothesis about whether it'll generalize. Discovered algorithms that come out as readable code, rather than opaque neural networks, have a real advantage here, because a human can look at it and say, "oh, that's just exploiting the fact that rewards are clipped," or "no, that's actually a genuinely new idea."

So I'm optimistic about automated research, I think it's going to massively accelerate things. But the bottleneck shifts. It moves from generating ideas to evaluating them honestly. Whoever gets evaluation right is going to get the real gains, and everyone else is going to produce very impressive numbers on benchmarks that don't mean much.

r001.rationale: It invokes Goodhart’s law, explaining that a strong optimizer aimed at a narrow benchmark proxy will exploit shortcuts and weaken the benchmark’s validity.

r002.rationale: It says that repeated human research iterations on a handful of benchmarks already create collective overfitting, even without dishonesty.

r003.rationale: It ties whether a discovered algorithm is genuine progress to transfer beyond its meta-training distribution, including to held-out, structurally different environments.

r004.rationale: It recommends held-out environments that are ideally structurally different, but does not ask which axes of generalization should distinguish meta-training from meta-testing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's genuinely one of the failure modes that worries me most about the whole "AI scientist" direction, and it's a bit subtle.

The way I'd frame it is this. Benchmark overfitting has always been a problem in RL. We've known for years that the field has a bit of a Goodhart problem, right? Atari, MuJoCo, then Procgen, and so on. People tune hyperparameters, they tune seeds, and you end up with methods that look great on the benchmark and then don't transfer. But historically there was a natural rate limiter on this, which is that humans are slow and somewhat lazy. A PhD student can only run so many experiments before they get bored or run out of compute or their advisor tells them to write it up. That friction, as annoying as it is, was actually doing some work in keeping the search process honest, or at least honest-ish.

Now, when you automate the research loop, you remove that friction. An agent, or a population of agents, can do thousands of iterations of propose-implement-evaluate against a fixed benchmark. And the thing you have to remember is that this is literally an optimisation process. If your objective is "score on benchmark X," you're going to get something that maximises score on benchmark X. That's what optimisers do. Any gap between the benchmark and the thing you actually care about, which is generality, robustness, scientific insight, will get exploited. It's basically reward hacking, but one level up. It's reward hacking of the scientific process itself.

And I'd actually argue it's worse than the classic version, for a couple of reasons. One, the search is much more powerful, so it finds the cracks faster. Two, the artefacts that come out are harder to audit. If a human overfits, you can sort of read the paper and go, hmm, that seems suspicious. If an automated system generates a weird algorithm with twenty bespoke tweaks that happen to work on this benchmark suite, it's really hard to tell whether there's a real idea in there or whether it's just stitched together a bunch of exploits.

So what do you do about it? A few things I think matter.

First, held-out evaluation has to become a first-class thing, and I mean genuinely held out, not "we didn't tune on the test set very much." The automated system should never see the environments you ultimately judge it on. And ideally those environments are themselves being generated or changing over time, so that the thing you're measuring is closer to the ability to generalise rather than performance on a static target. There's a nice connection here to open-endedness and unsupervised environment design, which is stuff we've worked on. If the distribution of tasks is itself growing and shifting, it's just much harder to overfit to.

Second, I think we should be asking the systems to produce not just methods but explanations and predictions. If an algorithm discovery pipeline says, "here's a new update rule," I want it to also say, "and here's why I think it works, and here's what I predict it will do in this other setting it hasn't been run in." Then you can test the prediction. Science isn't just about hitting a number. It's about understanding, and understanding is precisely the thing that generalises. If the only output is a score, you've already lost.

Third, and this is maybe the more philosophical point, I think we need to be a bit careful about what we're even trying to automate. There's a version of automated research that's just hyperparameter search with extra steps. That's fine, it's useful, but let's not pretend it's science. And there's a more ambitious version where the system is proposing hypotheses, designing experiments to discriminate between them, and updating. That second thing is much more robust to overfitting because the experiments are being chosen to be informative rather than to maximise a score. I think that's where the interesting work is, and honestly, I think it's also where the safety-relevant work is, because a system that's optimising for understanding behaves very differently from a system that's optimising for a leaderboard.

And then the last thing I'd say is that the community norms matter. We already have this issue where a lot of what gets published is noise, because of seed variance and so on. If we start accepting results from automated pipelines with the same lax standards, we'll just get noise at scale. So things like the Rliable-style statistical rigour, many seeds, reporting confidence intervals, that has to be baked in from the start, not bolted on afterwards.

So the short version is, yes, I think the risk is real and it's actually quite severe, but it's not a reason not to do this. It's a reason to be thoughtful about the objective. The whole game in RL is that you get what you optimise for. That lesson applies to automating RL research just as much as it applies to RL itself.

r001.rationale: It calls benchmark optimization a Goodhart problem and explains that optimizing a benchmark score exploits gaps between the benchmark and the goals it is meant to measure.

r002.rationale: It says researchers tune hyperparameters and seeds, producing methods that perform well on benchmarks but fail to transfer.

r003.rationale: It ties the value of automated research to generality and robustness, and recommends evaluating whether discovered methods work in unseen settings.

r004.rationale: It advocates held-out and changing environments, but does not ask which axes should distinguish meta-training from meta-testing.

astra-6.text:
I think the danger is that we automate the process of getting better at benchmarks without getting better at the underlying problems. You can overfit a benchmark even if no individual training run ever sees the test set. If you repeatedly use the results to decide which algorithms to keep, which ideas to pursue, and which experiments to run next, then the research process itself is effectively training on that benchmark.

Automation potentially makes that much faster. And in reinforcement learning, there are so many choices—the environment distribution, the reward function, the amount of tuning, the compute budget—that an apparent algorithmic improvement can be quite difficult to disentangle from a better search over those choices.

So I’d want us to evaluate the research process, not just its winning algorithm. Freeze the method, give it genuinely new tasks, and ask whether the improvement survives. Ideally, those tasks should require something meaningfully different, rather than just a new random seed. And account for the cost of discovering the method, not only the cost of running it once you know what works.

The exciting possibility is that automation lets us test ideas much more broadly. But that only helps if we use it to try to falsify our claims, rather than just to squeeze another percentage point out of the same leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response describes benchmark overfitting when research choices are repeatedly guided by benchmark results, but it does not invoke Goodhart’s law or clearly frame the issue as a measure losing validity when optimized.

r002.rationale: It says repeated use of benchmark results can make the research process overfit, but does not specifically observe that human researchers’ trial-and-error optimization already causes this.

r003.rationale: It proposes freezing the method and checking whether gains survive on genuinely new, meaningfully different tasks, framing progress in terms of transfer beyond the tasks used to develop it.

r004.rationale: It recommends testing on different tasks, but does not ask which generalization axes should separate meta-training from meta-testing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the danger is that you automate the outer loop as well as the inner loop. You’re no longer just training a policy to do well on a benchmark; you’re searching over algorithms, architectures, and research ideas to do well on that same benchmark. Even if each individual experiment is perfectly legitimate, the whole process can overfit.

And then the question is: what have we actually learned? Have we found a general principle that makes reinforcement learning work better, or have we found something that happens to exploit the particular set of environments we keep evaluating on?

So I’d want to separate the environments used to develop a method from the environments used to assess the resulting scientific claim. And that separation needs to happen at the level of task families, not just random seeds. A new seed is useful, but it doesn’t tell you whether your algorithm generalizes to a substantially different problem.

Automation could actually help here, because it can make broader testing much cheaper. But we have to make that breadth part of the objective. If we just automate the pursuit of a single leaderboard number, we’ll get very efficient at producing leaderboard improvements whose meaning is increasingly unclear.

r001.rationale: It says optimizing a single leaderboard number can make the resulting improvements’ meaning unclear, conveying that the benchmark loses value as a measure when it becomes the target.

r002.rationale: It discusses overfitting from automating research, but does not observe that human researchers’ trial-and-error optimization already causes benchmark overfitting.

r003.rationale: It questions whether an automated discovery is a general improvement or only exploits evaluated environments, and calls for assessing generalization to substantially different problems.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes development from assessment environments and specifies task families, rather than random seeds, as the relevant basis for that separation.
